items.followUp: Define a molecule and classify molecules as homoatomic or heteroatomic, giving two examples of each.

rubric.why: The definition identifies a molecule as an independently existing particle that retains the substance’s chemical properties.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as the smallest particle that can exist independently and retain the substance’s chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition containing the key ideas of smallest particle, independent existence and retention of chemical properties.

rubric.why: These identify two types classified by the number of atoms and give examples.
rubric.description: Describes monoatomic and diatomic molecules with examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each correct type with a suitable example: monoatomic (e.g. He) and diatomic (e.g. O₂).

rubric.why: These identify the remaining two types classified by the number of atoms and give examples.
rubric.description: Describes triatomic and polyatomic molecules with examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each correct type with a suitable example: triatomic (e.g. O₃) and polyatomic (e.g. P₄).

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, helium (He).
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, oxygen (O₂).
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, ozone (O₃).
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, phosphorus (P₄).

items.followUp: State one limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model and explain how Bohr’s model addressed it.

rubric.why: The definition describes a quantum as a discrete amount or packet of energy.
rubric.description: Defines a quantum as a discrete packet or fixed amount of energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a quantum as a discrete packet or fixed amount of energy.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model has electrons revolving around the nucleus and fails to account for atomic stability.
rubric.description: States Rutherford’s model of electrons revolving around the nucleus and its stability problem: the electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electron-around-nucleus model and 1 mark for the stability problem.

rubric.why: Bohr’s fixed, non-radiating energy levels and energy changes during transitions distinguish his model from Rutherford’s.
rubric.description: States that electrons occupy fixed energy levels and do not radiate energy in them; they absorb or emit energy when moving between levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed, non-radiating energy levels and 1 mark for absorption or emission of energy during transitions.

modelAnswer: A quantum is a fixed, discrete packet of energy that an atom can absorb or emit.
Rutherford proposed that electrons revolve around a small, positively charged nucleus.
According to Rutherford’s model, revolving electrons should continuously lose energy and fall into the nucleus; therefore, it could not explain atomic stability.
Bohr proposed that electrons occupy only certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus.
Electrons do not radiate energy while in these stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when they move between energy levels.
